Subject: Pilot packaging question: seat vs throughput model

Hey Karthik / Lauren,

Quick one — as we scope the upcoming pilot I want to make sure we understand the tradeoffs between running CareLogix on a seat-based model (developer seats + API quota) versus a throughput commit (reserved token throughput / sustained QPS). Our primary concerns: predictable latency for clinical inference during business hours, and a clean downgrade path if we don't hit the expected volume after 6 weeks.

Specific asks:
- Which packaging gives the clearest rollback/crediting mechanics?
- How do feature bundles (priority routing, KV caching, streaming) map to the two approaches?
- Any recommended guardrails to avoid surprise charges during burst testing?

We'll share the security questionnaire this afternoon. Can we get a short one-page recommendation and a sample pricing sheet?

Thanks,
Tom Benson

Subject: Re: Pilot packaging question: seat vs throughput model

Tom — thanks for the clear asks. Quick summary first, then a recommended pilot approach.

Short answer: hybrid reserved throughput + small seat pool.

Rationale and details:
- Rollback/credits: Throughput commits are easier to meter and return credits for unused committed capacity (we prorate monthly). Seat-based entitlements are simpler for access control but harder to translate to token-level credits. If your priority is a clean downgrade path with measurable unit economics, start with a small throughput commit for production traffic and keep a handful of dev seats for integrations/alerts.
- Feature mapping: priority routing, prefix KV caching, and streaming are all supported under either model. However, priority routing is tied to the committed tier (higher SLOs require a throughput pledge). KV caching reduces per-token cost and should be enabled by default for both modes.
- Burst guardrails: enable burst buckets and hard caps on per-project QPS; configure automated fallback to a lower-cost model variant (quantized at 8-bit) when burst thresholds are crossed. We'll include suggested threshold values in the pricing sheet.

Recommended pilot plan (6 weeks):
1) Reserved throughput: commit to a conservative steady-state of X tokens/min (we'll propose numbers after the workshop).
2) Seat pool: 8 developer seats for integrations, triage, and evaluation.
3) Discount: pilot discount applied to throughput commit (proposal below) with a refund/credit schedule if commit utilization < 40% at the end of pilot.
4) Rollback: option to convert unused committed tokens into a 3-month credit at 60% value or move to a seat-based arrangement with prorated adjustments.

I'll attach a concise pricing sheet and a draft SOW. Can we schedule a 45-minute workshop with your platform team this week?

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
karthik_iyer@redwood.com

Tom — adding a couple of commercial guardrails from our side so expectations are clear: 

Pilot commercial terms suggestion:
- Pilot length: 6 weeks.
- Pilot discount: 15% off the listed throughput rate for the committed tier (applies to committed throughput only).
- Utilization credit: If average committed utilization across the pilot < 40%, Redwood will issue a credit equal to 60% of the unused commit value, applied to future invoices.
- Downgrade window: within 30 days of pilot end, CareLogix may request a one-time conversion of remaining commit to seats (prorated for remaining term).

Operational notes:
- We'll include explicit throttles and a hard cap to prevent runaway burst charges; all caps are configurable by you via the console and require a single point of contact to raise.
- SOW will list which features are included in the pilot (priority routing, KV caching, streaming, observability retention for 30 days). Add-ons (longer retention, private VPC) are priced separately.

I'll mark up the SOW with these commercial bullets and send back this morning.
